challenges.title: Two Sum
challenges.prompt:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indexes of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Every input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the smaller index first.
hints: At index i, which exact value would you need to have seen earlier?
Store each value's index in a map as you go, and check for the complement target - nums[i] before storing.
challenges.explanation: One pass with a map from value to index. For each number, check whether its complement was already seen; if so, the stored index is the smaller one. Checking before storing stops an element from pairing with itself.

challenges.title: Contains Duplicate
challenges.prompt: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice, and `false` if every value is distinct.
hints: Checking every pair works but is O(n^2).
Keep a set of the values seen so far and check it before adding each new value.
challenges.explanation: A set answers "have I seen this?" in O(1) on average. Return true at the first repeat; if the loop finishes, every value was new. Sorting and comparing neighbors is an O(n log n) alternative that needs less extra memory.

challenges.title: Valid Anagram
challenges.prompt: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`: it uses exactly the same letters, each the same number of times, possibly in a different order. Otherwise return `false`.

examples.explain: Both have three a's and one each of g, m, n and r.
t has a c and no t.

constraints: s and t contain lowercase English letters
hints: Two strings of different lengths can never be anagrams.
Count each letter of s, then subtract the letters of t. Any count that goes negative means t has an extra letter.
challenges.explanation: With equal lengths, t is an anagram exactly when it never needs a letter that s has run out of. Count s up, then count t down and fail on the first shortage. Sorting both strings and comparing also works in O(n log n).

challenges.title: Group Anagrams
challenges.prompt: Given a list of lowercase words, group together the words that are anagrams of each other. Return a list of groups. The groups, and the words inside each group, may be in any order.

examples.explain: eat, tea and ate share the letters a, e, t.
One empty word forms one group.

hints: What could you compute from a word that is identical for all of its anagrams?
Sorting a word's letters gives such a key: "tea" and "eat" both become "aet".
Use a map from key to a list of words, then return the map's values. In JavaScript the key must be a string.
challenges.explanation: Anagrams have the same sorted letters, so that string is a canonical key. One pass appends each word to the list for its key. A tuple of 26 letter counts is an O(k) key if words are long.

complexity.time: O(n k log k) for n words of length up to k

challenges.title: Top K Frequent Elements
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` values that appear most often. The answer is guaranteed to be unique, and you may return the values in any order.

Aim for better than O(n log n).
constraints: The set of top k values is unique
hints: Start by counting how often each value appears.
Sorting the distinct values by count works in O(n log n). A heap of size k gives O(n log k).
For O(n), make buckets indexed by frequency (no value appears more than n times) and collect values from the highest bucket down.
challenges.explanation: Count every value, then place each value in a bucket indexed by its count. Walking the buckets from the highest frequency down yields values in order of frequency, so the first k collected are the answer. Every step is linear.

challenges.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
challenges.prompt:
Given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers that all appear in it (in any positions). Duplicates count once.

Aim for O(n) time.
hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). To beat it, put every value in a set for O(1) membership checks.
A number x starts a run only if x - 1 is not in the set.
From each run start, walk x + 1, x + 2, ... while they are present. Each number is walked at most once overall.
challenges.explanation: Put everything in a set. Only numbers whose predecessor is missing start a run, and only those walk upward, so every number is visited by a walk at most once. That keeps the nested loop at O(n) in total.
